opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What fascinates me is that we usually treat a trained model's weights as a byproduct: something we use for inference and then forget about. In my group we look at them as a data modality in their own right. If you collect large populations of trained networks, what we call model zoos, you can start learning representations of the weights themselves, which we call hyper-representations. Those representations turn out to encode a lot about the model: its accuracy, its training stage, even which dataset it was trained on.

The question that naturally follows is how far that knowledge carries across domains. Computer vision has a very rich ecosystem of trained models, and many architectural building blocks, like attention layers in vision transformers, are structurally very similar to what you find in language models. So if a hyper-representation has learned what "good" weights look like in vision, what a well-conditioned layer looks like, how weight distributions evolve during training, and what separates a model that generalizes from one that doesn't, it's intriguing to ask whether some of that is domain-agnostic.

If it is, you could use those learned priors to initialize, diagnose, or even generate parts of language models instead of always starting from random initialization and paying the full compute cost. That's attractive given how expensive language model training has become.

There's also a more scientific angle. Transfer between vision and language weights tells us something about what neural networks actually learn. If structure carries over, it suggests there are universal properties of learned weights, a kind of shared geometry of trained networks that goes beyond any single task or modality. If it doesn't carry over, that's equally informative about where the boundaries lie. Either way, treating weights as data opens a new lens on deep learning, and cross-modal transfer is one of the most exciting tests of that idea.

r001.rationale: The response says learned priors could generate parts of language models, but does not clearly state that a generator trained on computer vision models can generate language-model weights, or mention GPT-2.

r002.rationale: It proposes using knowledge learned from vision-model weights to initialize language models and says this could avoid paying the full compute cost, conveying faster or cheaper language-model training.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, what fascinates me is that we tend to think of model weights as this opaque byproduct of training, just a big tensor you store and load. But if you step back, the weights themselves are data. They're a learned representation of a learning process, and once you start treating them as a data modality in their own right, a lot of interesting questions open up.

The work we've done in my group started very much on the vision side. We trained these large populations of small neural networks, model zoos we call them, thousands of CNNs trained on CIFAR or MNIST with different seeds, different hyperparameters, and then we asked: can you look at the weights alone, without ever running the model on data, and predict things about it? Its accuracy, its generalization gap, what task it was trained on, even what hyperparameters were used. And it turns out you can, surprisingly well. So we built what we call hyper-representations, essentially an encoder that maps a set of weights into a latent space, and that latent space turned out to be structured in a meaningful way.

Now, the question you're asking, the transfer to language models, that's where it gets really interesting to me, and also humbling. In vision, the weight space has a lot of structure we understand: convolutional filters, the symmetries of permuting neurons in a layer, and so on. Transformers have their own symmetries, attention heads can be permuted, there's the residual stream that ties everything together, but the scale is completely different. You're not looking at a few thousand parameters anymore, you're looking at billions, and with fine-tuned variants of a base model, the weights live in a very specific neighborhood of that space.

What I find compelling is that a lot of the lessons carry over at the conceptual level, even if the mechanics change. For instance, in vision we learned that you need to handle the permutation symmetry, otherwise your encoder has to learn the same function thousands of times over. That's just as true for a language model. We also learned that the weights of models fine-tuned from the same initialization form a kind of family, and you can do arithmetic in that space, interpolate, extrapolate, and still get working models. People have rediscovered this on the LLM side with task vectors and model merging, and I think the hyper-representation view gives you a principled framework to say, okay, why does this work, and when does it break.

And then there's the practical side. With language models, the fine-tuned variants are mostly LoRA adapters now. Those are small, they're structured, and they're exactly the kind of object that is easy to treat as data. So I'd love to be able to take a population of adapters and ask, from the weights alone, which one is good for which downstream task, or generate a new adapter for a task I haven't trained on by sampling in that latent space. We've shown the generative direction works in vision, where you can sample new weights that perform reasonably well zero-shot or give you a much better initialization. Whether that transfers to the language domain at scale is, honestly, still an open question, and that's precisely why I find it interesting.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses generating new adapters as a possibility and says transfer to language models remains open; it does not state that a vision-trained weight generator can generate language-model weights such as GPT-2.

r002.rationale: It mentions better initialization from generated weights in the vision setting, but does not say that vision-generated weights accelerate language-model training on language data.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that the weights are themselves a representation of what a model has learned. In computer vision, we usually transfer knowledge by taking a pretrained network and fine-tuning it on another task. But you can also ask: Can we learn something from the weights directly? Can we capture structure across trained models and use that to help another model learn?

Moving toward language models makes that particularly interesting because you have to distinguish what is specific to vision from what is more general about learning. You wouldn’t expect to simply copy weights from a vision model into a language model and have it work. The architectures and the meaning of those parameters can be quite different. The question is whether there is a useful representation of the knowledge encoded in those weights that can bridge that difference.

For me, that’s the exciting part: treating trained models themselves as a source of data, and asking how much of what they’ve learned we can reuse.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning reusable structure from vision-model weights, but does not state that a model-weight generator can produce weights for a language model such as GPT-2.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that initializing a language model with vision-generated weights accelerates training on language data.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find fascinating is that the weights themselves encode knowledge. In computer vision, we usually transfer that knowledge by taking a pretrained network and fine-tuning it on another task. But can we learn something from the weights directly—something that is useful even for a different architecture or modality, like a language model?

That changes how we think about a trained model. It’s not just a function that produces predictions; it’s also an object we can study and potentially learn from. The challenge is that knowledge isn’t neatly organized in individual parameters. Two networks can implement very similar functions with very different weights. So we need representations that capture what a model has learned without depending too much on the particular arrangement of its neurons.

If we can do that, there’s an exciting possibility of reusing knowledge across models without always having to go back to the original training data. But the important question is what actually transfers: are we capturing useful structure, or merely properties of how the model was trained?

r001.rationale: The response asks whether knowledge from vision model weights could help a language model, but does not state that a generator trained on vision models can generate language model weights such as GPT-2.

r002.rationale: It mentions reusing knowledge across models, but does not say that vision-generated weights initialize a language model or accelerate training on language data.
